newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia problems mount ahead of Yeltsin's comeback.
newsitem.headline: Russia problems mount ahead of Yeltsin's comeback.

text.p: As President Boris Yeltsin prepares to return to the Kremlin after months of illness, problems facing Russia are mounting on all fronts.
Doctors and the Kremlin say the 65-year-old leader is recovering quickly after his heart bypass operation on November 5.
On Monday, he moved to the Rus residence, a hunting lodge of former Soviet leaders to combine "work and active recreation".
But earlier plans to deliver a radio or television address to the nation have been apparently dropped and most political analysts agree that Yeltsin wants to reappear in public at his best.
"Being overjoyed that the operation was a success, the Kremlin wants to sell it at the highest price," said Sergei Parkhomenko, editor of the influential Itogi weekly magazine.
"They want Yeltsin not just to reappear but to come back full of energy, decisions and initiatives. His return should be full of pomp and fireworks," Parkhomenko told Reuters.

Yeltsin was away from the Kremlin for long spells last year due to heart problems. This year he put them aside in February to concentrate on the election campaign which left him little if any time at all to run affairs of state.
Having won four more years in power, Yeltsin never really returned to the Kremlin and went under the surgeon's knife.
The latest date of his expected return to work was given last week as December 25.
On the one hand, the fact that nothing really dramatic has happened while Yeltsin was away appears to be a sign of a certain political stabilisation in Russia.
But on the other hand, because the constitution gives president immense powers, a barrage of unresolved problems has been mounting during his absence.
It is especially noticable in foreign relations where Russia, its honeymoon with the West over, is trying to find a new global role.
Increasingly isolated on the issue, Moscow is waging a losing battle against NATO plans to expand eastwards.
"The main question for the next year is -- will Yeltsin come back strongly or not," said a Moscow-based western diplomat recently.
"At present there is nobody to do business with in Moscow. Everybody is waiting for his return because someone has to say: "This is the way we need to do things'."
Yeltsin clearly feels this and has already arranged meetings with the leaders of the United States, Germany and France.
Russia's economy is also a headache for Yeltsin.

While the government resists firmly pressure from some members of parliament and lobby groups to print more money, it has so far failed to come up with a solution over how to pay a huge backlog of pensions and salaries.
Up to now, the government has found no effective means to collect taxes, which leaves its coffers bare.
Because of the logjam, the International Monetary Fund has delayed October and November payments of a $10 billion three-year loan to Russia.
The 1997 budget is yet to be approved by the State Duma (lower chamber of parliament) where the opposition, led by the communists, forms a majority.
Not all is quiet on the political front, though the communists have not recovered fully after a defeat of their leader in the presidential election.
The opposition is fighting strongly in elections of regional governors who are also members of the upper house of parliament.
One of the biggest problems for Yeltsin, said Parkhomenko, was that he could not make any further use of one weapon that served him so well in the election campaign.
"He cannot promise anything now because people will remember how many promises he has made during the election campaign and broke after winning."
